top.headline: Musk's America PAC bets anti-trans ads will drive GOP turnout in four Senate races
top.blurb: Elon Musk's America PAC is targeting Democratic Senate candidates in Ohio, Iowa, Texas and Alaska with ads over transgender athletes and gender-transition care, part of a get-out-the-vote drive Musk has authorized to spend upward of $100 million on. The heavy emphasis on trans issues marks a notable shift in how Republican Senate campaigns have run this cycle.

top.headline: Sununu and Pappas set up a marquee New Hampshire Senate race for Shaheen's open seat
top.blurb: Former senator John Sununu easily beat Trump ally-turned-primary-rival Scott Brown for the GOP nomination, while Rep. Chris Pappas turned back a Democratic Socialist challenge from Karishma Manzur. The November matchup for retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen's seat is one of the cycle's most competitive, in a state that hasn't elected a Republican senator in 16 years.

top.headline: Police are combing Flock's camera network to chase down 'loitering' and 'vagrancy'
top.blurb: Records from the small town of Plano, Illinois show police departments as far as Georgia have searched its Flock cameras over 1,200 times under the category 'Curfew/Loitering/Vagrancy Violations,' not for any specific crime. Flock's nationwide network of 120,000-plus cameras lets any department search by category rather than by suspect, turning ordinary presence in public into a searchable offense.

more.headline: Inside the secretive donor network positioning JD Vance for 2028
more.blurb: Rockbridge, the secretive donor network Vance co-founded in 2019, drew Cabinet secretaries, senators and Silicon Valley financiers to a Dallas reception ahead of the GOP's midterm convention.

top.headline: Supreme Court pushes toward a pan-India safety audit of student housing after Satya Niketan
top.blurb: A Supreme Court bench declined the solicitor general's request to leave the Satya Niketan collapse, which killed seven, to the Delhi High Court, saying building safety 'has to be on a pan-India basis.' The amicus has proposed a nationwide audit of PG accommodations and hostels checking sanctioned plans, floor counts, fire safety and whether structures are in a dangerous condition.

top.headline: US destroys five Iranian tankers; Iran fires missiles at a US base in Jordan
top.blurb: The US said it sank five Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Kharg Island, prompting Iran to fire 20 ballistic missiles at Jordan's Al-Azraq air base; Jordan's military says it intercepted all but two, which fell in open ground. Iran also struck ten more ships near the Strait of Hormuz, part of a tanker war that has now hit at least 75 vessels since fighting began.

top.headline: Rubio closes a three-nation Latin America tour meeting Peru's new government
top.blurb: The secretary of state closed a swing through Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, all three now led by leaders aligned with the Trump administration, with meetings in Lima on trade, security cooperation against narcotrafficking and earthquake relief. It is Washington's clearest recent push to consolidate a friendlier bloc in a region it has often struggled to hold.

top.headline: Pakistan collapse to 133 all out as England seize control of the series decider
top.blurb: Pakistan were skittled for 133 on the opening day of the third and final Test at Edgbaston, with Josh Tongue taking 4 for 42 and debutant wicketkeeper Ghazi Ghori out for four. Babar Azam, without a Test century in nearly four years, fell for seven, and England replied with an unbeaten 156 for 4 at stumps behind fifties from Emilio Gay and Harry Brook.

top.headline: Colin Kaepernick on losing football, Jay-Z and what protest taught him about power
top.blurb: A decade after first taking a knee, Kaepernick tells NPR's Michel Martin he has no regrets, reflecting in his new memoir 'The Perilous Fight' on growing up the adopted Black son of a white family, the costs of his sport, and his disappointment with Jay-Z's NFL partnership. The book spans the years around the 2016 season that ended his career and began his activism.

bengal.headline: Heavy rain floods Malda, triggers landslides across north Bengal's hill districts
bengal.blurb: Relentless rain since Wednesday night submerged parts of Malda district and triggered landslides near Siliguri, prompting a red alert for Darjeeling, Kalimpong and three other hill districts with tourists stranded.

travel.headline: A sake tour of Japan, from centuries-old houses to experimental small breweries
travel.blurb: Lonely Planet tours Japan's nihonshu breweries, from centuries-old houses in Kyoto and Hiroshima to smaller producers experimenting with wild yeasts and unfiltered styles.

travel.headline: First genome of any Philippine endangered mammal maps a path to save the Visayan spotted deer
travel.blurb: Scientists sequenced the first draft genome of any Philippine endangered mammal from a captive Visayan spotted deer, mapping 2.5 billion DNA letters to help guide the roughly 700 left in the wild.

happy.headline: A 2,000-year-old scroll buried by Vesuvius has been read from beginning to end without ever being opened
happy.blurb: AI pattern-recognition on X-ray scans let researchers virtually unroll a carbonized Herculaneum scroll intact, revealing previously unknown writings by the Epicurean philosopher Philodemus on vices and on the gods.

tech_top.headline: Apple unveils its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo
tech_top.blurb: Apple's 'Surprise and Shine' event introduced the iPhone Duo, a book-style foldable with a 5.4-inch outer display and 7.6-inch inner screen, running on a new in-house C2 modem that further reduces Apple's reliance on Qualcomm. It arrives October 23 at $1,999, alongside a refreshed iPhone 18 Pro line, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5.
tech_top.pm_note: Apple built its own modem and hinge specifically to make a two-screen device work — a reminder that owning your hardware supply chain, not just clever software, is what turns a novelty form factor into something shippable at scale.

tech_top.headline: US intelligence agencies accuse six Chinese AI firms of 'industrial-scale' distillation of American models
tech_top.blurb: A joint NSA, CISA and FBI advisory says DeepSeek, Alibaba, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, StepFun and Z.AI pulled billions of tokens from Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's GPT, Google's Gemini and xAI's Grok to train their own models, using fraudulent accounts and proxy 'transfer stations' to evade detection. Rather than blocking flagged accounts outright, the agencies recommend providers quietly degrade responses to suspected distillation traffic.
tech_top.pm_note: When an intelligence advisory can name your product's outputs as another company's training data, abuse detection and terms-of-service enforcement stop being a policy footnote and become a security control regulators will expect you to have.

tech_more.headline: Marvel's Doctor Doom crashed a Seattle council meeting to praise its surveillance cameras
tech_more.blurb: A person dressed as the Marvel supervillain Doctor Doom thanked the Seattle City Council for expanding surveillance camera proposals, a stunt aimed at drawing attention to how far the city's plans have advanced.

tech_101.text: The mechanical and software work needed to make a screen bend thousands of times without a visible crease or a weak point. Apple's iPhone Duo uses a custom liquid-metal hinge and its own C2 modem, built in-house rather than bought from suppliers.

Training a smaller AI model by having it learn from a larger one's outputs — legitimate when done with permission, but a terms-of-service violation when done by scraping a rival's responses at scale, as US agencies allege several Chinese firms have done.

science.headline: A hidden atomic structure, not metallic nickel, may be what actually converts methane
science.blurb: Chinese researchers found that a tiny, previously overlooked atomic structure forming on nickel oxide during methane conversion is more catalytically active than the metallic nickel long assumed to drive the reaction. Correcting the mechanism could help chemists design cheaper, more efficient catalysts for turning methane into higher-value chemicals.

science.headline: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS is unusually rich in methanol
science.blurb: New observations of the interstellar visitor 3I/ATLAS found exceptionally high levels of methanol relative to water, far more than typical solar-system comets carry. The composition suggests the comet formed under chemical conditions unlike those that shaped most comets born around our own sun.

science.headline: Ozempic and Wegovy linked to sharply fewer asthma and COPD attacks
science.blurb: A study of more than 80,000 UK patients found semaglutide, the drug in Ozempic and Wegovy, was linked to nearly 40% fewer asthma attacks and about 20% fewer COPD flare-ups than other diabetes treatments. Researchers say GLP-1 drugs may carry respiratory benefits beyond diabetes and weight loss, though clinical trials are still needed to confirm it.

philosophy.headline: Why 'hard choices' aren't about finding the objectively better option
philosophy.blurb: Philosopher Ruth Chang argues that genuinely hard choices aren't cases where one option is secretly better and we just can't see it, but cases where options are 'on a par' — comparable without being equal. She suggests the way through is introspective: asking which option you could commit to and stand behind, rather than searching for a tiebreaker that doesn't exist.

philosophy.headline: We don't have different perspectives on reality — we inhabit different realities
philosophy.blurb: Sociologist Steve Fuller argues that treating disagreement as a matter of differing 'perspectives' on one shared reality undersells how differently people's frameworks actually carve up the world. Drawing on ideas from quantum mechanics and epistemology, he suggests some disagreements are less about interpretation than about which reality someone is effectively operating in.

philosophy_101.text: Philosopher Ruth Chang's term for options that are comparable in value without being equal or one being strictly better — the reasoning problem behind decisions like choosing a career, where standard comparison breaks down.

The idea that what counts as true or real depends on a particular standpoint or framework, rather than there being one neutral view from nowhere. Steve Fuller pushes this further, arguing people aren't just seeing reality differently but inhabiting different ones.
